entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

input.content:
# zarrow perf round 4: no more per-row fallbacks for take/filter/concat

Patch: `perf4.patch` (LF, `git apply` on HEAD 362ecf1; checked with `git apply --check` on a
`git archive HEAD` tree). Files: `src/compute/datum_permutation.zig`, `src/concat_array_refs.zig`,
`src/compute/test_datum.zig`, two new benchmarks, `tools/benchmark_ci_check.py`,
`tools/test_benchmark_ci_check.py`, `tools/benchmark_ci_thresholds.json`. `build.zig` needs no
change: it registers every `benchmarks/*_benchmark.zig` (run, smoke, full, matrix, ci steps).

## Root causes

1. `datumTakeArrayLikeNullable` only had kernels for fixed width, bool, string/binary and
   list/large_list. Everything else made one `slice(idx, 1)` per index (an ArrayRef node, a
   children array, retained buffers) or `buildNullLikeArray(type, 1)` per null index, then a
   concat of N one-row parts. Base: struct 3,500-4,000 ns/row, fixed_size_list ~2,000 ns/row.
   Dictionary, sparse union, list_view did not work at all (`UnsupportedType`): `concatTwoArrayRefs`
   had no dictionary/union/view arm and `buildNullLikeArray` has no dictionary case. Fixed-size
   binary also took the per-row path (`takeFixedWidthArray` did not list it).
2. Chunked take resolved every index with a binary search, then emitted contiguous runs as slices
   and every other row as its own 1-row chunk (random take: one chunk per row, ~200 ns/row).
   `datumFilter` on a chunked datum used `datumElementArrayAt` (`lookupChunkAt`, O(chunks)) plus
   a concat per kept row (~75-100 ns/row).
3. `concatArrayRefs` for list/large_list/map/fixed_size_list/struct used a balanced pairwise
   merge: log2(parts) levels, each copying everything and allocating new nodes per pair
   (12,500 parts: 14 levels; 150-300 ns/row).

## Design

Take (`datum_permutation.zig`):
- `takeArray` dispatches on the storage layout (`storageDataType`, now `pub` in concat), so
  extension arrays take their storage layout and keep their own type. `hasTakeKernel` lists the
  layouts left on the per-row path: string_view, binary_view, dense_union, run_end_encoded.
- Fixed width: `fixedByteWidth` (factored out of `takeFixedWidthArray`) adds fixed_size_binary
  (arbitrary widths go through a `@memcpy` arm next to the inline 1/2/4/8/16/32 ones) and
  dictionary (index width). Dictionary take = index gather; the output shares (retains) the
  dictionary. Null indices are null with index 0.
- Struct and sparse union (`takeStructLikeArray`): validity by `gatherBits` (union: gather the
  type-id bytes; a null index gets the first declared type id), every child taken with the same
  indices through `takeChildren`, recursing into the kernels. Child coordinates follow
  `ArrayRef.slice`/`childCoversRange`: a child as long as the parent is row-aligned (row idx),
  otherwise it is in parent coordinates and is sliced to `[offset, offset + length)` first
  (one slice per child per take). Null struct rows keep their child rows (as arrow-rs does);
  null indices produce null child rows, which is exactly what the old per-row path produced
  (`buildNullLikeArray` builds null children), so child validity is consistent with the oracle.
- Fixed-size list: validity by `gatherBits`. A fixed-width child (not bool/dictionary) is copied
  per list row with one `@memcpy` of `size * width` bytes and its validity bits set one by one
  (`takeFixedSizeListValues`). Other children are taken once with expanded indices
  `(offset + idx) * size + k` (`takeExpandedChild`; dense indices expand to u32 when the child
  fits, `?usize` indices expand null to null child rows).
- map = `takeListArray(i32)` (the child is the entries struct, which now has a kernel).
- list_view/large_list_view: gather offsets and sizes (each bounds-checked against the child);
  the child is shared, not copied (arrow-rs does the same).
- null type: checkIndices + a null array of the output length.
- `takeListArray` now uses `takeChildren` (shared child-take helper). The empty-index early
  return moved after the kernels, so a zero-length take of a type without a
  `datumBuildEmptyLike` case (double, decimal, dictionary...) now works instead of
  `UnsupportedType`; types without a kernel keep the old empty builder.
- Chunked take (`takeChunked`): prefix sums of chunk lengths; `chunkOf` (hint + binary search)
  maps an index to its chunk. A first pass counts runs of indices that stay in one chunk and stops
  as soon as there are more than total/64 runs (ponytail-marked constant). Many runs (random
  take): concat the chunks once (N-ary) and run the flat kernel. Few runs (filters, sorted or
  clustered takes): copy indices to chunk-local ones and take each run from its chunk with the
  array kernels. If the chunks do not concat (e.g. different dictionaries per chunk) the per-run
  path is used. The pieces are returned in order; `datumTakeChunkedNullable` makes them the output
  chunks (no concat; this keeps chunks with different dictionaries working), the array-output
  callers concat them once. Layouts without a kernel keep a per-row path (one 1-row slice per
  index), which preserves the old chunked behaviour for dense unions, REE and views.
- Filter: `datumFilter` keeps the dense-u32 selection path (predicate array + drop_nulls) for
  every datum form; otherwise `datumFilterSelectionIndices`. Both end in `takeAsArray`
  (array: kernels; chunked: `takeChunked` + one concat; scalar: the unchanged per-row path).
  The old per-row predicate loops (and `appendOwnedArrayRef`, `flushTake*`) are deleted.
  `datumFilterChunkAware` and `datumTake` on chunked datums go through `takeChunked` too (no more
  `?usize` copy of dense indices).

Concat (`concat_array_refs.zig`):
- `concatManyNested` (list, large_list, map, fixed_size_list, struct, and extensions of them):
  pass 1 over the parts checks the type (`std.meta.eql` first, since parts sliced from one array
  share the type's pointers; then `dataTypeEql`), the buffer/child counts, sums rows and records
  every child's window (`Part{ref, start, len}`: list = offsets range via `offsetsRange`,
  checked against the child length; fixed_size_list = rows * list_size; struct = row-aligned or
  parent coordinates, the `ArrayRef.slice` rule). Pass 2 writes validity (`appendValidityBits`)
  and rebased list offsets (`rebaseOffsets`, split out of `copyBinaryPart`; checked against
  i32/i64 max). Each child is then concatenated once from its windows (`concatParts`: flat
  N-ary, nested N-ary recursively, else slices + `concatArrayRefs`). `validateLayout` on the
  result as before. The nested path does its own type check, so `concatArrayRefs` skips its
  separate type-check loop for nested layouts (one fewer pass over the part nodes).
- `concatManyFlat` takes ArrayRefs or windows (`partData`: a whole-array window is read in place,
  a partial window is an `ArrayData.slice` on the stack) and handles dictionaries whose parts
  share one dictionary node (index concat, dictionary retained). Different dictionaries return
  null and fall through to the pairwise path's `UnsupportedType`, as before.
- The pairwise list/fixed_size_list/struct helpers (`concatListLikeArrayI32/I64`,
  `concatFixedSizeListArray`, `concatStructArray`, `sliceStructChildRef`, `nullCountForArray`,
  `concatValidityBuffer`) are deleted; the pairwise merge remains for string_view/binary_view.

What made the 16-row-part concat fast enough: the first N-ary version handed children down as
full `ArrayData` copies (200 B per window) and was at ~20 ns/row for the struct shape. rdtsc
profiling showed the time in pass 1, and a run that reused the scratch across calls cut it in
half: on Windows the multi-MB scratch arrays were fresh pages every call (page faults). Windows
of 24 B (ref, start, len) bring the struct shape to ~9-11 ns/row. A per-node type check
(`dataTypeEql` per part) cost ~15 ns/row on its own; `std.meta.eql` first removes that.

## Trust boundaries

- Indices: `checkIndices` in every new kernel (struct/union, fsl, list_view, null, chunked).
- Offsets read from arrays: list_view offset+size checked against the child length per taken row;
  list windows in concat use `offsetsRange` (bounds and monotone ends) and the rebased offsets go
  through `validateLayout`; fixed_size_list and struct child windows are checked against the
  child length; sparse-union type ids buffer length is checked; overflow checks on every size
  product.
- The fuzz `compute` target (take/filter/concat/slice on decoded data, `validateFull` on every
  result) is the oracle. Two bugs found by it during the round, both fixed: a zero-field struct
  indexed an empty window list in concat pass 2 (fuzz corpus `c-abi` input), and a partially
  built children slice was freed with the wrong length on an error path.

## Tests (3 new, 378 total on 0.16 and 0.17)

`src/compute/test_datum.zig`, oracle = `rowsEqual` (logical row i of the output equals row
indices[i] of the source, recursing through struct/list/map/list_view/fsl/dictionary/union/
extension), i.e. the definition of the per-row path:
- "datumTake nested kernels match the per-row oracle on sliced inputs with null indices": 13
  sources (struct, struct with parent-coordinate children, dictionary, fsl<int32>, fsl<string>
  (expanded-index path), fixed_size_binary, extension, map, list_view, sparse union, struct
  without fields, null, list<struct>) x {full, sliced(1, n-1)} x {nullable indices with nulls,
  dense indices}, `validateFull` on every result, out-of-range index rejected.
- "concatArrayRefs N-ary nested path matches the source rows for sliced parts": the same sources
  cut into sliced parts (including an empty part); union and list_view must still be
  `UnsupportedType` (unchanged).
- "chunked take and filter run the array kernels per chunk and match the flat result": sorted
  indices (per-chunk path) and scattered indices (concat-first path) with nulls, filter with
  drop_nulls true/false vs the flat filter, and a chunked dictionary with different dictionaries
  per chunk (concat-first fails, per-run pieces become the output chunks).

## Verification (final code)

- `zig build test -j2`: 378/378 on 0.17 and 0.16 (`--cache-dir .zig-cache16`).
- `zig build fuzz-corpus -j2`: all six targets replay clean on 0.17 and 0.16.
- 0.16 `zig fmt --stdin` (CR stripped) clean on all touched .zig files.
- `python tools/test_benchmark_ci_check.py`: 16 tests OK; `zig build benchmark-ci` CSV passes
  `benchmark_ci_check.py` and `benchmark_ci_regression_check.py`.
- `tools/fuzz.py --optimize ReleaseSafe run --targets compute,array-layout,c-abi --seconds 180`
  (fresh .fuzz-out): see the summary at the end.

## Benchmarks

New: `benchmarks/take_nested_benchmark.zig` (200k rows x 80 iterations; struct{int32,string},
dictionary<int32,string> 16 values, fixed_size_list<int32,4>, the int32 column as 16 chunks:
random take and ~50% filter, plus the same filter on the flat column as the reference) and
`benchmarks/concat_nested_benchmark.zig` (list<int32> 0-3 items/row and struct{int32,string}, cut
into 12,500 parts of 16 rows). CSV names: `take_nested_{struct,dictionary,fixed_size_list,
chunked_take,chunked_filter,flat_filter}`, `concat_nested_{list,struct}`.

Method: `ab4.sh` (in the scratchpad) builds both trees (0.17 ReleaseFast) and alternates
base/new runs. The base tree runs the same benchmark files with a base-only hack: the per-row
cases run 4 iterations instead of 80 (they take seconds per iteration) and an unsupported case
reports its error. The machine was shared with other jobs (CPU load 50-99 %), so the A/B numbers
carry noise; flat benchmarks are the control.

## Skipped

- dense_union and run_end_encoded take: still the per-row path, which fails with
  `UnsupportedType` as before (no concat for them either). Dense union needs per-child index
  lists and offset rewriting, REE needs run search + new run ends: neither is the small
  same-pattern addition.
- string_view/binary_view: still per-row (slices + builder concat, works, slow).
- Union/list_view/REE concat: unchanged (`UnsupportedType`).
- Chunked takes of contiguous runs used to be zero-copy slices; they are now copied by the
  kernels (one piece per chunk run). Correct, cheaper for everything but the identity take.

change: it registers every `benchmarks/*_benchmark.zig` (run, smoke, full, matrix, ci steps).

## Root causes

1. `datumTakeArrayLikeNullable` only had kernels for fixed width, bool, string/binary and
   list/large_list. Everything else made one `slice(idx, 1)` per index (an ArrayRef node, a
   children array, retained buffers) or `buildNullLikeArray(type, 1)` per null index, then a
   concat of N one-row parts. Base: struct 3,500-4,000 ns/row, fixed_size_list ~2,000 ns/row.
   Dictionary, sparse union, list_view did not work at all (`UnsupportedType`): `concatTwoArrayRefs`
   had no dictionary/union/view arm and `buildNullLikeArray` has no dictionary case. Fixed-size
   binary also took the per-row path (`takeFixedWidthArray` did not list it).
2. Chunked take resolved every index with a binary search, then emitted contiguous runs as slices
   and every other row as its own 1-row chunk (random take: one chunk per row, ~200 ns/row).
   `datumFilter` on a chunked datum used `datumElementArrayAt` (`lookupChunkAt`, O(chunks)) plus
   a concat per kept row (~75-100 ns/row).
3. `concatArrayRefs` for list/large_list/map/fixed_size_list/struct used a balanced pairwise
   merge: log2(parts) levels, each copying everything and allocating new nodes per pair
   (12,500 parts: 14 levels; 150-300 ns/row).

## Design

Take (`datum_permutation.zig`):
- `takeArray` dispatches on the storage layout (`storageDataType`, now `pub` in concat), so
  extension arrays take their storage layout and keep their own type. `hasTakeKernel` lists the
  layouts left on the per-row path: string_view, binary_view, dense_union, run_end_encoded.
- Fixed width: `fixedByteWidth` (factored out of `takeFixedWidthArray`) adds fixed_size_binary
  (arbitrary widths go through a `@memcpy` arm next to the inline 1/2/4/8/16/32 ones) and
  dictionary (index width). Dictionary take = index gather; the output shares (retains) the
  dictionary. Null indices are null with index 0.
- Struct and sparse union (`takeStructLikeArray`): validity by `gatherBits` (union: gather the
  type-id bytes; a null index gets the first declared type id), every child taken with the same
  indices through `takeChildren`, recursing into the kernels. Child coordinates follow
  `ArrayRef.slice`/`childCoversRange`: a child as long as the parent is row-aligned (row idx),
  otherwise it is in parent coordinates and is sliced to `[offset, offset + length)` first
  (one slice per child per take). Null struct rows keep their child rows (as arrow-rs does);
  null indices produce null child rows, which is exactly what the old per-row path produced
  (`buildNullLikeArray` builds null children), so child validity is consistent with the oracle.
- Fixed-size list: validity by `gatherBits`. A fixed-width child (not bool/dictionary) is copied
  per list row with one `@memcpy` of `size * width` bytes and its validity bits set one by one
  (`takeFixedSizeListValues`). Other children are taken once with expanded indices
  `(offset + idx) * size + k` (`takeExpandedChild`; dense indices expand to u32 when the child
  fits, `?usize` indices expand null to null child rows).
- map = `takeListArray(i32)` (the child is the entries struct, which now has a kernel).
- list_view/large_list_view: gather offsets and sizes (each bounds-checked against the child);
  the child is shared, not copied (arrow-rs does the same).
- null type: checkIndices + a null array of the output length.
- `takeListArray` now uses `takeChildren` (shared child-take helper). The empty-index early
  return moved after the kernels, so a zero-length take of a type without a
  `datumBuildEmptyLike` case (double, decimal, dictionary...) now works instead of
  `UnsupportedType`; types without a kernel keep the old empty builder.
- Chunked take (`takeChunked`): prefix sums of chunk lengths; `chunkOf` (hint + binary search)
  maps an index to its chunk. A first pass counts runs of indices that stay in one chunk and stops
  as soon as there are more than total/64 runs (ponytail-marked constant). Many runs (random
  take): concat the chunks once (N-ary) and run the flat kernel. Few runs (filters, sorted or
  clustered takes): copy indices to chunk-local ones and take each run from its chunk with the
  array kernels. If the chunks do not concat (e.g. different dictionaries per chunk) the per-run
  path is used. The pieces are returned in order; `datumTakeChunkedNullable` makes them the output
  chunks (no concat; this keeps chunks with different dictionaries working), the array-output
  callers concat them once. Layouts without a kernel keep a per-row path (one 1-row slice per
  index), which preserves the old chunked behaviour for dense unions, REE and views.
- Filter: `datumFilter` keeps the dense-u32 selection path (predicate array + drop_nulls) for
  every datum form; otherwise `datumFilterSelectionIndices`. Both end in `takeAsArray`
  (array: kernels; chunked: `takeChunked` + one concat; scalar: the unchanged per-row path).
  The old per-row predicate loops (and `appendOwnedArrayRef`, `flushTake*`) are deleted.
  `datumFilterChunkAware` and `datumTake` on chunked datums go through `takeChunked` too (no more
  `?usize` copy of dense indices).

Concat (`concat_array_refs.zig`):
- `concatManyNested` (list, large_list, map, fixed_size_list, struct, and extensions of them):
  pass 1 over the parts checks the type (`std.meta.eql` first, since parts sliced from one array
  share the type's pointers; then `dataTypeEql`), the buffer/child counts, sums rows and records
  every child's window (`Part{ref, start, len}`: list = offsets range via `offsetsRange`,
  checked against the child length; fixed_size_list = rows * list_size; struct = row-aligned or
  parent coordinates, the `ArrayRef.slice` rule). Pass 2 writes validity (`appendValidityBits`)
  and rebased list offsets (`rebaseOffsets`, split out of `copyBinaryPart`; checked against
  i32/i64 max). Each child is then concatenated once from its windows (`concatParts`: flat
  N-ary, nested N-ary recursively, else slices + `concatArrayRefs`). `validateLayout` on the
  result as before. The nested path does its own type check, so `concatArrayRefs` skips its
  separate type-check loop for nested layouts (one fewer pass over the part nodes).
- `concatManyFlat` takes ArrayRefs or windows (`partData`: a whole-array window is read in place,
  a partial window is an `ArrayData.slice` on the stack) and handles dictionaries whose parts
  share one dictionary node (index concat, dictionary retained). Different dictionaries return
  null and fall through to the pairwise path's `UnsupportedType`, as before.
- The pairwise list/fixed_size_list/struct helpers (`concatListLikeArrayI32/I64`,
  `concatFixedSizeListArray`, `concatStructArray`, `sliceStructChildRef`, `nullCountForArray`,
  `concatValidityBuffer`) are deleted; the pairwise merge remains for string_view/binary_view.

What made the 16-row-part concat fast enough: the first N-ary version handed children down as
full `ArrayData` copies (200 B per window) and was at ~20 ns/row for the struct shape. rdtsc
profiling showed the time in pass 1, and a run that reused the scratch across calls cut it in
half: on Windows the multi-MB scratch arrays were fresh pages every call (page faults). Windows
of 24 B (ref, start, len) bring the struct shape to ~9-11 ns/row. A per-node type check
(`dataTypeEql` per part) cost ~15 ns/row on its own; `std.meta.eql` first removes that.

## Trust boundaries

- Indices: `checkIndices` in every new kernel (struct/union, fsl, list_view, null, chunked).
- Offsets read from arrays: list_view offset+size checked against the child length per taken row;
  list windows in concat use `offsetsRange` (bounds and monotone ends) and the rebased offsets go
  through `validateLayout`; fixed_size_list and struct child windows are checked against the
  child length; sparse-union type ids buffer length is checked; overflow checks on every size
  product.
- The fuzz `compute` target (take/filter/concat/slice on decoded data, `validateFull` on every
  result) is the oracle. Two bugs found by it during the round, both fixed: a zero-field struct
  indexed an empty window list in concat pass 2 (fuzz corpus `c-abi` input), and a partially
  built children slice was freed with the wrong length on an error path.

## Tests (3 new, 378 total on 0.16 and 0.17)

`src/compute/test_datum.zig`, oracle = `rowsEqual` (logical row i of the output equals row
indices[i] of the source, recursing through struct/list/map/list_view/fsl/dictionary/union/
extension), i.e. the definition of the per-row path:
- "datumTake nested kernels match the per-row oracle on sliced inputs with null indices": 13
  sources (struct, struct with parent-coordinate children, dictionary, fsl<int32>, fsl<string>
  (expanded-index path), fixed_size_binary, extension, map, list_view, sparse union, struct
  without fields, null, list<struct>) x {full, sliced(1, n-1)} x {nullable indices with nulls,
  dense indices}, `validateFull` on every result, out-of-range index rejected.
- "concatArrayRefs N-ary nested path matches the source rows for sliced parts": the same sources
  cut into sliced parts (including an empty part); union and list_view must still be
  `UnsupportedType` (unchanged).
- "chunked take and filter run the array kernels per chunk and match the flat result": sorted
  indices (per-chunk path) and scattered indices (concat-first path) with nulls, filter with
  drop_nulls true/false vs the flat filter, and a chunked dictionary with different dictionaries
  per chunk (concat-first fails, per-run pieces become the output chunks).

## Verification (final code)

- `zig build test -j2`: 378/378 on 0.17 and 0.16 (`--cache-dir .zig-cache16`).
- `zig build fuzz-corpus -j2`: all six targets replay clean on 0.17 and 0.16.
- 0.16 `zig fmt --stdin` (CR stripped) clean on all touched .zig files.
- `python tools/test_benchmark_ci_check.py`: 16 tests OK; `zig build benchmark-ci` CSV passes
  `benchmark_ci_check.py` and `benchmark_ci_regression_check.py`.
- `tools/fuzz.py --optimize ReleaseSafe run --targets compute,array-layout,c-abi --seconds 180`
  (fresh .fuzz-out): see the summary at the end.

## Benchmarks

New: `benchmarks/take_nested_benchmark.zig` (200k rows x 80 iterations; struct{int32,string},
dictionary<int32,string> 16 values, fixed_size_list<int32,4>, the int32 column as 16 chunks:
random take and ~50% filter, plus the same filter on the flat column as the reference) and
`benchmarks/concat_nested_benchmark.zig` (list<int32> 0-3 items/row and struct{int32,string}, cut
into 12,500 parts of 16 rows). CSV names: `take_nested_{struct,dictionary,fixed_size_list,
chunked_take,chunked_filter,flat_filter}`, `concat_nested_{list,struct}`.

Method: `ab4.sh` (in the scratchpad) builds both trees (0.17 ReleaseFast) and alternates
base/new runs. The base tree runs the same benchmark files with a base-only hack: the per-row
cases run 4 iterations instead of 80 (they take seconds per iteration) and an unsupported case
reports its error. The machine was shared with other jobs (CPU load 50-99 %), so the A/B numbers
carry noise; flat benchmarks are the control.

## Skipped

- dense_union and run_end_encoded take: still the per-row path, which fails with
  `UnsupportedType` as before (no concat for them either). Dense union needs per-child index
  lists and offset rewriting, REE needs run search + new run ends: neither is the small
  same-pattern addition.
- string_view/binary_view: still per-row (slices + builder concat, works, slow).
- Union/list_view/REE concat: unchanged (`UnsupportedType`).
- Chunked takes of contiguous runs used to be zero-copy slices; they are now copied by the
  kernels (one piece per chunk run). Correct, cheaper for everything but the identity take.

def build(args):

    cmd = ["zig", "build", "fuzz-install", f"-Doptimize={args.optimize}", "-j2"] + args.zig_args
    print("+", " ".join(cmd), flush=True)

def cmd_run(args):
    targets = TARGETS if args.targets == "all" else args.targets.split(",")
    build(args)
    for target in targets:
        tdir = args.out / target
        tdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        deadline = time.monotonic() + args.seconds
        execs_note = 0
        while (left := deadline - time.monotonic()) > 1:
            chunk = int(min(args.chunk, left))
            seed = random.randrange(1 << 62)
            corpus = ROOT / "fuzz" / "corpus" / CORPUS.get(target, target)
            cmd = [str(args.exe), target, "run", f"{chunk}s", "--corpus", str(corpus), "--out", str(tdir),
                   "--seed", str(seed), "--max-len", str(args.max_len)]
            kind, text = supervise(cmd, args, wall=chunk + 30 + 2 * args.timeout)
            execs_note += 1
            if kind:
                data = (tdir / "current.bin").read_bytes() if (tdir / "current.bin").exists() else b""
                save(args.out, target, kind, data, text)
            else:
                print(f"[{target}] " + (text.strip().splitlines() or ["(no output)"])[-1], flush=True)
    return 0


def cmd_replay(args):
    build(args)
    files = []
    for p in map(Path, args.paths):
        files += sorted(f for f in p.iterdir() if f.is_file()) if p.is_dir() else [p]
    findings = 0
    for f in files:
        if f.stat().st_size > 1 << 20:
            continue
        kind, text = supervise([str(args.exe), args.target, "replay", str(f.resolve())], args, wall=2 * args.timeout + 5)
        if kind:
            findings += 1
            save(args.out, args.target, kind, f.read_bytes(), f"input: {f}\n" + text)
    print(f"[{args.target}] replayed {len(files)} files, {findings} findings", flush=True)
    return 1 if findings and args.fail else 0

| chunked take | 184 | 2.7–3.5 | ≤2x flat (2.0) ✓ |

The existing take, filter and concat benchmarks are unchanged within noise.

**What changed in behaviour:**
- **Now works:** take on dictionary, sparse union and list_view used to fail with `UnsupportedType`. A zero-length take of types like double or decimal used to fail too.
- **Chunked outputs:** a chunked take now returns one piece per chunk run instead of zero-copy slices. That is a copy for the identity-take case. Chunks with different dictionaries still work: when the chunks can't be concatenated, the take falls back to one piece per run.
- **Null struct rows** keep their child rows, as arrow-rs does. Null indices produce null child rows, the same as the old per-row path.
- **Concat** of list/struct/fixed_size_list/map no longer uses the pairwise merge; that code is deleted. Dictionary concat works when all parts share one dictionary, otherwise it returns `UnsupportedType` as before.

**Verification on the final code:**
- `zig build test -j2`: 378/378 on 0.17 and 0.16 (375 existing + 3 new). The new tests compare each output row against the source row through a recursive per-row oracle, over 13 layouts, full and sliced inputs, null indices, the chunked paths, and a different-dictionaries chunked case.
- `zig build fuzz-corpus -j2` is clean on both compilers; 0.16 `zig fmt` is clean on all touched files.
- `python tools/test_benchmark_ci_check.py` passes, and `zig build benchmark-ci` produces CSV that passes both CI checkers.
- **Fuzz, 180 s per target, fresh `.fuzz-out`:** compute and array-layout had no findings. c-abi recorded one `hang | |` with no stack frames. The saved input and `current.bin` replay clean in 0.5 s, and an unpatched HEAD run the same way records the same signature, so I'm treating it as the known supervisor/load artifact rather than something this patch introduced.
- The fuzz corpus caught one real bug during the round, now fixed: struct concat with zero fields indexed past an empty array. I also fixed a wrong-length free on an error path.

**Decisions worth knowing:**
- Chunked take counts runs of indices that stay in one chunk. Random indices concatenate the chunks once and use the flat kernel; sorted indices and filters take each run from its own chunk. The 64-rows-per-run threshold is marked `ponytail:`.
- For the 16-row concat, the biggest cost turned out to be fresh scratch pages on Windows. That is why the per-part child window records are 24 bytes and not full `ArrayData` copies.
- The concat type check runs `std.meta.eql` before `dataTypeEql`, because a full struct type compare per part cost about 15 ns/row on its own.

**Left on the old path:** dense_union and run_end_encoded take (still `UnsupportedType`, as before; neither was a small addition in the same pattern), string_view/binary_view take (still per row, works), and concat for union/list_view/REE (unchanged).
